theory.title: Closures
theory.content:
A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its outer (enclosing) scope even after that outer function has returned.

How it works

When a function is created in JavaScript, it captures a reference to its surrounding lexical environment — all variables in the scope where it was defined. This combination of the function and its lexical scope is called a closure.

function counter() {
  let count = 0;
  return function() {
    count++;
    return count;
  };
}

const increment = counter();
console.log(increment()); // 1
console.log(increment()); // 2
console.log(increment()); // 3

Common use cases

  • Data encapsulation — hiding private state inside a function
  • Factory functions — creating functions with preconfigured behavior
  • Memoization — caching the results of expensive computations
  • Callbacks and event handlers — preserving context from the outer scope

theory.title: Prototype and Inheritance
theory.content:
JavaScript uses prototype-based inheritance. Every object has an internal link to another object called its prototype. When you access a property that doesn't exist on an object, the engine traverses the prototype chain to find it.

Prototype chain

const animal = {
  speak() {
    return `${this.name} makes a sound`;
  }
};

const dog = Object.create(animal);
dog.name = 'Rex';

console.log(dog.speak()); // Rex makes a sound
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === animal); // true

ES6 Classes

Classes are syntactic sugar over prototypal inheritance:

class Animal {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  speak() {
    return `${this.name} makes a sound`;
  }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
  speak() {
    return `${this.name} barks`;
  }
}

const dog = new Dog('Rex');
console.log(dog.speak()); // Rex barks

theory.title: Event Loop
theory.content:
JavaScript is single-threaded but handles asynchronous operations through the event loop — a mechanism that continuously checks whether the call stack is empty and then processes queued tasks.

Execution order

console.log('1'); // synchronous

setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0); // macrotask

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3')); // microtask

console.log('4'); // synchronous

// Output: 1, 4, 3, 2

Key rule

After each macrotask, the engine processes all pending microtasks before moving to the next macrotask. This is why Promise callbacks always run before setTimeout callbacks, even with a 0 ms delay.

theory.title: Promises and Async/Await
theory.content:
A Promise is an object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation. It can be in one of three states: pending, fulfilled, or rejected.

Async/Await

async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises that makes asynchronous code look and behave like synchronous code:

async function loadUsers() {
  try {
    const users = await fetchData('/api/users');
    return users.filter(u => u.active);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Error:', err);
  }
}

Promise combinators

  • Promise.all() — waits for all promises; rejects if any rejects
  • Promise.allSettled() — waits for all; returns results regardless of outcome
  • Promise.race() — resolves/rejects with the first settled promise
  • Promise.any() — resolves with the first fulfilled promise

theory.title: this keyword
theory.content:
In JavaScript, this refers to the execution context — the object that is currently calling the function. Its value is determined at runtime, not at definition time (except for arrow functions).

Rules for determining this

  1. Global context — this is window (browser) or global (Node.js)
  2. Method call — this is the object before the dot: obj.method()
  3. Explicit binding — call, apply, or bind set this explicitly
  4. Constructor call — new Func() sets this to the newly created object
  5. Arrow functions — inherit this from the enclosing lexical scope
